sense: a time: before it is out

evidence: Plaut. Curc. 448: subēgit sōlus intrā vīgintī diēs
Liv. 36.10.1: intrā decimum diem quam Pherās vēnerat
terms.comment: Sets the limit: before the time is out. With quam, within so many days of an event (Liv. 36.10.1, Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: construction: the length of time in the ablative, with no preposition
evidence: Cic. Att. 9.14.2: quicquid est bīduō sciēmus
Cic. Fam. 7.4: mē hōc bīduō aut trīduō exspectā
terms.comment: The everyday way in Cicero’s letters: paucīs diēbus, in a few days; hōc bīduō, in the next two days. It answers “how soon?”; intrā stresses that the time will not be overrun.

phrases.latin: dīmidiam partem nātiōnum ūsque omnium subēgit sōlus intrā vīgintī diēs
phrases.english: single-handed, within twenty days, he conquered half of all the nations there are

phrases.latin: Cūrā igitur ut valeās, et mē hōc bīduō aut trīduō exspectā.
phrases.english: So take care of your health, and expect me within the next two or three days.
whatever it is, we shall know within two days

phrases.latin: sed nunc properō. perscrībam ad tē paucīs diēbus omnia.
phrases.english: But I am in a hurry now; I’ll write you the whole story in a few days.

biduum.against: Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked (s.v. biduus)
biduum.html: As in trīduum, which Lewis & Short marks long. De Vaan 173, s.v. diū: the long ī of bīduum, trīduum, which Walde–Hofmann explain from postrīdiē and de Vaan perhaps from bīmus.

sources: Lewis & Short: intra · Lewis & Short: biduus · Lewis & Short: triduum
